r: This one-credit review course exists solely to renew Red Cross Professional Rescuer certification through supervised skill practice and graded proficiency testing in chest compressions, AED pad placement and shock delivery, and rescue breathing on manikins under time pressure. The instrumental work task is psychomotor and situational, not informational: correct compression depth and rate, airway positioning, and coordinated two-rescuer sequencing demonstrated live to a certified evaluator. Task-exposure research places manual, physical work at the low end of automation exposure, and nothing about generative AI substitutes for a body performing graded compressions or shocking a manikin correctly under an instructor's direct observation. Certification renewal is contractually tied to in-person demonstrated proficiency, not a written score alone, so the course's entire instrumental purpose is embodied testing. Over the next 24 months no deployable system removes that requirement.

By 2031 AI tools may enrich preparation for this recertification, e.g., adaptive quizzing on written protocol changes or simulated scenario walkthroughs, but the credential itself will almost certainly still require live skill demonstration, because Red Cross certification standards and most employer/licensure downstream requirements for professional rescuers rest on directly observed psychomotor competence, not written assessment. The course's binding constraint is verification burden: an AI system cannot certify that a specific human can deliver adequate chest compression depth on a real body in an emergency, and error costs there are irreducibly high. Task-exposure research's finding that manual and physical work resists automation should still hold at this horizon; capability trend data describing fast-improving task-time horizons in digital domains does not translate into robotic CPR proxies replacing certified human rescuers in the field. Expect continuity, with AI as an ancillary study aid at most.

A ten-year horizon invites more hedging, but even generous assumptions about robotics and simulation-based training do not obviously eliminate the instrumental need for a human to be personally certified as a competent physical rescuer, since professional-rescuer roles (lifeguards, camp staff, allied health support) will still require an individual, not an institution's AI system, to respond bodily to a cardiac or airway emergency in the room. Capability trend research shows fast doubling of digital task-time horizons, but embodied, real-time, high-stakes physical performance under an evaluator remains a distinct capability class largely untouched by those trends so far. It is plausible some written-knowledge components migrate toward AI-assisted review, but the graded hands-on skill test binding this specific course to a specific certification is likely to persist, so a confident prediction of elimination is not warranted.
ESS 1010.d: This course is designed for students who have the interest or need to maintain CPR/AED for the Professional Rescuer level certification but do not require a full course. The review format is organized as an abbreviated course that briefly reviews course information and offers students the opportunity for skill practice prior to testing. Certification requirements are 80% on all written tests and demonstrated skill proficiency. Successful completion of this course will renew CPR/AED for the Professional Rescuer certification for two (2) years. To participate in a review course a student must be currently certified in CPR/AED for the Professional Rescuer or the equivalent. Certification will be verified at the first class meeting. This is a Red Cross Certification.

r: Physical Well-being surveys practical content on sleep, nutrition, exercise, resilience, and stress management aimed at a general student audience, with the instrumental task being synthesis and personal application of broad wellness information rather than clinical intervention. Much of this content already resembles what consumer AI assistants deliver competently: summarized nutrition guidance, sleep-hygiene checklists, and generic stress-reduction routines are exactly the kind of writing and information-synthesis tasks that task-exposure research associates positively with automation exposure. Still, at 24 months classroom delivery, discussion, and personalized accountability from an instructor retain real value that a chatbot answer does not replicate for most students, and verification burden is nontrivial since bad personalized health advice has real costs. The course is not licensure- or GT-Pathways-gated, so no institutional lock-in protects it; exposure is present but not yet dominant.

By 2031, consumer-grade AI wellness coaching, personalized nutrition and exercise plan generation, and conversational stress-management guidance are plausible mainstream deployments given the trajectory of the Anthropic Economic Index toward broad consumer usage in writing and everyday-task categories. Much of what this course transmits, general information about physical wellness domains and how they interrelate, is well within reach of digital delivery once diffusion catches up with capability, though Census BTOS diffusion data shows adoption still lagging capability broadly across firms and, by extension, informal educational contexts. Verification burden remains moderate rather than low: personalized health-adjacent advice benefits from human judgment about individual circumstances, providing some protective friction. No accreditation or licensure constraint holds this course in place, so its instrumental rationale weakens materially if AI wellness tools become a normalized substitute for this kind of general instruction.

Ten years out, it is plausible that AI-mediated personal wellness coaching, delivered through consumer apps capable of adaptive, ongoing guidance rather than a single semester of lecture content, substantially displaces the instrumental function of a standalone introductory wellness course for many students, particularly given how strongly writing- and information-synthesis-heavy tasks track with automation exposure in current research. However, this is a genuine hedge rather than a confident forecast: adoption diffusion has historically lagged raw capability, macro-level productivity effects from AI have so far been modest, and student engagement, accountability, and behavior-change motivation may still benefit from structured in-person instruction in ways a chat interface underdelivers. With no institutional lock-in and no strongly protective verification burden, this course has fewer structural defenses against long-run substitution than clinically gated or heavily embodied ESS offerings, warranting a Medium rather than Low rating.
ESS 1030.d: In this course, students learn practical information about physical well-being. Students focus on improving all aspects of physical wellness and mental health to include adaptability, resilience, sleep, nutrition, exercise, and stress management. This course is designed to interest the general student body, which wants to learn more about the correlation between well-being and overall health.

r: Stress Management Techniques teaches the physiological and psychological elements of stress-induced conditions alongside practical management strategies, an instrumental blend of conceptual health knowledge and applied technique instruction such as breathing, relaxation, or cognitive-behavioral-style coping methods. At 24 months, generic strategy content of this kind is readily reproduced by AI chat assistants, which already generate competent explanations of stress physiology and standard coping techniques; this matches the observed-usage pattern of writing and informational tasks dominating consumer AI use. However, effective stress-management instruction depends on modeling, guided practice, and individualized feedback that a static AI response does not fully replace in a live classroom setting, and the course carries no licensure or GT-Pathways designation that would otherwise lock it in place. Near-term instrumental need remains real but only modestly protected.

By 2031, expect wider availability of AI-guided stress-management tools, adaptive relaxation coaching apps, and conversational cognitive-behavioral exercises that approximate much of this course's technique-delivery function, consistent with the trend of AI usage concentrating in writing, coaching-style, and self-help-adjacent content categories. The underlying knowledge, stress physiology and generic coping strategies, is not verification-heavy in the way clinical intervention is, since misapplication of a breathing exercise carries low error cost compared to, for example, a misdiagnosed medical condition. That relatively low verification burden means less structural protection against substitution than more clinically gated ESS coursework. Diffusion research indicates adoption of such tools across institutions and individuals will likely lag raw model capability, tempering how quickly this shifts, but the course's instrumental case weakens as personalized AI coaching becomes normalized among the population it serves.

At the ten-year horizon it becomes plausible that individualized, always-available AI stress-coaching substantially reduces the instrumental need for a dedicated introductory course transmitting generic technique knowledge, since capability-trend research documents fast-improving task-time horizons for exactly this kind of conversational, low-verification-burden guidance. This is offered as a hedge, not a certainty: institutional and cultural adoption of AI as a primary stress-management resource is uneven, and some students will still value structured, cohort-based instruction and accountability that a chatbot session does not replicate. No accreditation or foundational-prerequisite constraint holds the course in the curriculum against this pressure, so its Medium rating reflects genuine long-run exposure tempered by the same diffusion lag and behavior-change limitations that slow adoption of self-help AI tools generally, rather than any structural or licensure-based protection specific to this course.
ESS 1440.d: This course is designed to provide the student with an understanding of the elements of stress-induced conditions. The course provides strategies by which the student can learn to effectively manage stressful conditions.

r: Introductory Sports Medicine Concepts covers etiologies and basic care of musculoskeletal injuries such as fractures, sprains, strains, and contusions, alongside the injury assessment process itself, environmental illness recognition, emergency planning, risk reduction, and documentation. The instrumental task center is hands-on injury assessment, palpation, observation of mechanism and presentation, and real-time triage decisions, paired with accurate written documentation. This is embodied, real-time work close to the calibration anchor of hands-on clinical assessment: an AI system cannot palpate a joint or observe gait to determine injury severity on-site. Verification burden is meaningful because misjudging injury severity or missing an emergent condition carries real harm, requiring a knowledgeable human to check any AI-generated guidance. Documentation and general etiology knowledge are more exposed, but the assessment core anchoring the course keeps near-term instrumental need intact.

By 2031, AI-assisted documentation templates and etiology/reference lookups will likely be routine adjuncts for students and practitioners in this space, reflecting the strong positive association between writing/documentation tasks and automation exposure found in task-exposure research. But the physical, in-person component, palpating an injury, observing an athlete's movement pattern, gauging pain response, and deciding whether to activate an emergency action plan, remains resistant, matching task-exposure research's finding that manual and real-time interpersonal work sits at the low-exposure end even as capability elsewhere accelerates rapidly per METR/Epoch trend data. Verification burden stays real: an incorrectly triaged injury has direct health consequences, so a human capable of independent judgment must remain in the loop. The course's assessment-and-decision core is likely to remain instrumentally necessary, with only its peripheral knowledge-transmission elements meaningfully eroded.

Ten years out, some hedging is warranted around wearable sensors, computer vision, and AI-assisted diagnostic aids that could augment on-field injury assessment, potentially narrowing the gap between novice and AI-assisted judgment per productivity research showing AI uplift concentrated among less experienced workers. Even so, the embodied, real-time nature of hands-on injury evaluation and the emergency-response decision-making this course teaches is not obviously eliminable by 2036, since jagged-frontier research shows users relying on AI outside its competence become meaningfully less accurate, and mistriaging a musculoskeletal or environmental emergency carries exactly the high, non-obvious error cost that keeps verification burden low and protective. Diffusion of any such tools into introductory training settings will also likely lag their raw capability. A Low rating persists across all three horizons on the strength of this embodied, high-stakes assessment core.
ESS 1623.d: This course is designed to introduce students to etiologies, pathologies, and basic care of musculoskeletal injuries (e.g.; fractures, sprains, strains, contusions). Other topics covered in this course include the injury assessment process, environmental illnesses/injuries, emergency planning, risk reduction strategies and proper documentation.

r: Physical Literacy and Society blends conceptual instruction on physical literacy and its societal and wellness correlations with an applied component in which each student develops and executes a personalized wellness and physical-activity plan. The instrumental task is partly informational synthesis, explaining physical literacy's relationship to population health, and partly personal plan design and follow-through, which involves ongoing physical participation this semester. Task-exposure research finds writing- and synthesis-heavy tasks positively associated with exposure, which covers the conceptual half of this course, but the applied activity component keeps embodiment meaningfully present. The course carries a GT-Pathways Social and Behavioral Sciences designation, a statutory general-education transfer requirement that provides real, if not course-specific, institutional protection. At 24 months, near-term instrumental need remains intact given this gen-ed anchor and the activity requirement.

By 2031, AI tools generating individualized activity and wellness plans are plausible, reducing some of the instrumental case for instructor-guided plan design; this tracks the broader pattern of consumer AI usage concentrating in personalized writing and planning tasks per the Anthropic Economic Index. The conceptual content on physical literacy and its societal dimensions is similarly the kind of interpretive, synthesis-oriented material that AI already handles competently. The GT-Pathways designation, however, is a statutory 31-credit transfer-core requirement that keeps this course's general-education slot institutionally anchored regardless of how automatable its content becomes, capping erosion at Medium rather than allowing a slide to High. Verification burden remains moderate, not strongly protective, since a flawed AI-generated activity plan carries limited harm compared to clinical guidance, so exposure genuinely increases even as the course's curricular position holds.

At the ten-year horizon, further diffusion of AI into personalized fitness and wellness planning is plausible given capability-trend research on fast-improving task-time horizons, and the course's conceptual, synthesis-driven content likely becomes more substitutable for students who might otherwise seek this material independently. This is a hedge rather than a firm prediction: the GT-Pathways statutory designation is a durable structural constraint that does not depend on AI capability at all, meaning the course retains its curricular necessity for general-education completion even if its instrumental knowledge content becomes largely redundant with freely available AI tools. The physical-activity plan component also retains some embodied, participatory character that resists full digital substitution. The Medium rating at 5 and 10 years reflects real content exposure bounded by a firm, non-eroding institutional floor rather than a directional judgment about the discipline's value.
ESS 2021.d: This course allows the student to understand physical literacy and the impact of physical literacy on all populations and society across the world. Content covered includes the important correlation between physical literacy and overall wellness. A personalized approach is taken to assure students can gain the skills necessary to become physically literate and apply these skills throughout the semester and into the future. This course is part lecture and part activity as each student will develop and participate in their personal wellness and physical activity plan.

r: Emergency Rescue/First Responder & CPR prepares students to earn multiple Red Cross certifications, Medical Responder, Professional Rescuer CPR/AED, Blood Borne Pathogens, and Oxygen Administration, through hands-on skill acquisition in pulmonary resuscitation for infants, children, and adults plus equipment-based emergency care. The instrumental work task is embodied first-responder practice: airway management, resuscitation technique, bloodborne pathogen protocol compliance, and correct oxygen-delivery equipment operation, each requiring physical demonstration to a certified evaluator. Task-exposure research consistently places manual, physical, emergency-response work at the low end of automation exposure, and the certifying bodies behind each credential require direct observation of competence, not a written score. Verification burden is maximal given life-safety stakes. With four separate hands-on certifications bundled into one course, near-term instrumental necessity is essentially unaffected by AI capability.

By 2031, AI may support the didactic layer of this course, protocol updates, scenario-based quizzing, or documentation practice, but the certifying requirement for physically demonstrated resuscitation and equipment competence is unlikely to loosen, because Medical Responder, Professional Rescuer, and Oxygen Administration credentials are built around observed psychomotor performance under a qualified evaluator. This mirrors the calibration pattern seen in embodied clinical-assessment coursework, where verification burden stays low and protective regardless of how fast digital-task capability trends move elsewhere. Task-exposure research's manual-work exemption should still apply: no plausible near-term deployment lets an AI system certify that a specific person can correctly manage an airway or deliver oxygen therapy on a real patient. Expect the course's instrumental function to hold essentially unchanged, with AI serving only as ancillary study support.

A ten-year view invites appropriate hedging around advances in simulation technology and AI-assisted training feedback, which could make preparation for these certifications more efficient, but the core requirement, that a specific human physically perform and be evaluated on resuscitation and emergency-equipment skills, is not obviously removable given how far current robotics and embodied-AI capability trail the multimodal, real-time psychomotor competence required here. Capability trend research shows fast doubling of digital task-time horizons, but this course's binding constraint sits outside that domain almost entirely: certifying bodies tie credentials to directly observed human physical performance, and error costs from an incompetent responder remain severe. It would be overconfident to predict elimination of instrumental need by 2036; the more defensible position is continuity, with modest efficiency gains in preparation rather than any substitute for the certified skill itself.
ESS 2060.d: This course is designed for the professional and layperson to prepare them in emergency pulmonary resuscitation for infants, children and adults. This course will offer students the opportunity to develop skills and earn certifications in the following: American Red Cross Medical Responder, CPR/AED for the Professional Rescuer, Blood Borne Pathogens and Oxygen Administration.

r: Water Safety Instructor Certification trains students to teach water safety, including skill analysis and in-water correction of swimmers' technique, leading to Red Cross Water Safety Instructor certification, with required field-experience assignments. The instrumental work task is doubly embodied: instructors must both perform water-rescue and swimming skills competently and observe, diagnose, and physically correct another person's technique in real time in the water, a live psychomotor coaching task with drowning-prevention stakes. Task-exposure research places manual, physical, and real-time interpersonal instruction at the low end of automation exposure, and this course sits at an extreme of that category. Verification burden is maximal: an incorrectly certified water-safety instructor is a direct safety hazard. The prerequisite lifesaving certification and required field experience further anchor this as embodied, evaluator-verified training unaffected by near-term AI capability.

By 2031, AI might support the classroom-knowledge portion of instructor training, curriculum planning aids or written-test preparation, but the core instrumental task, observing a swimmer's stroke or a rescue technique in the water and correcting it through physical demonstration and real-time feedback, is not something current or near-term AI systems perform, since it requires embodied presence in the water alongside a physical body being taught. This tracks the manual-work exemption in task-exposure research even as capability elsewhere accelerates per METR/Epoch trend data. Verification burden remains low and protective because the Red Cross certifying body requires demonstrated in-water teaching competence, and the field-experience requirement embeds a supervised, real-world practicum component that resists digital substitution. Expect essentially unchanged instrumental necessity at this horizon.

Even with substantial hedging for advances by 2036, it is difficult to construct a plausible pathway by which AI eliminates the instrumental need for a human to be trained and evaluated in live, in-water swim instruction and rescue-skill correction, since this requires physical presence, tactile and visual real-time assessment, and hands-on correction of another person's body position and technique in the water, capabilities well outside current embodied-AI and robotics trajectories despite fast general capability trends. The required field-experience component further embeds this course in supervised practicum structures that are institutionally, not just technically, resistant to substitution. While some administrative or written-exam elements could migrate toward AI assistance, the embodied instructional core keeps this course's instrumental necessity intact; a confident prediction of disruption by 2036 is not supported by the available evidence.
ESS 2160.d: This course studies the methods of teaching water safety, skill analysis, and correction. Course leads to Red Cross Water Safety Instructor Certification. Field experience assignments will be a required part of the class.

r: Wellness Coaching I introduces scope of practice, ethics and values, effective communication, relationship-building, and research-based behavior-change facilitation as the core competencies of wellness coaching practice. The instrumental work task centers on real-time interpersonal coaching conversation: building rapport, applying motivational and behavior-change techniques, and navigating client ethics in the moment, activities the rating framework treats as embodied, real-time interpersonal work with low automation exposure at this horizon. While AI wellness-coaching chatbots exist and are growing in consumer use per Anthropic Economic Index usage data, the relationship-building and live judgment this course teaches, and that professional scope-of-practice standards presuppose a human coach exercising, are not yet substitutable at scale. Near-term instrumental need for structured, supervised training in this interpersonal skill set remains intact.

By 2031, AI-driven coaching and behavior-change apps are likely to be considerably more capable and more widely deployed, consistent with productivity research showing customer-support-style interactions gaining the largest AI-assisted improvements for less experienced practitioners. This raises real exposure for the informational and technique-based portions of wellness coaching curricula. However, the real-time, interpersonal relationship-building this course centers as core content remains a protected category under the framework's embodiment factor, and professional ethics/scope-of-practice training presumes a human exercising judgment in ambiguous situations, which keeps verification burden from collapsing to fully AI-safe. Numbered as a first course in a likely sequence, it also plays a foundational role for further coaching coursework. The balance of rising technique-automation against durable interpersonal and foundational protections keeps this course at Low rather than higher exposure.

At the ten-year horizon, it is plausible that AI coaching tools substantially absorb the informational and even some conversational-technique elements of wellness coaching, given capability-trend research on fast-improving task-time horizons and growing enterprise deployment of AI in coaching-adjacent domains. This justifies moving to Medium rather than staying Low, but real hedging is warranted: the course's foundational role in a coaching sequence and its emphasis on live relationship-building, ethics, and in-the-moment judgment are exactly the kind of real-time interpersonal work that task-exposure research and the embodiment factor treat as resistant, even as capability elsewhere accelerates. Whether AI coaching displaces the instrumental need for human-delivered wellness coaching training by 2036 depends heavily on client trust and regulatory developments this analysis cannot confidently predict, so Medium reflects genuine uncertainty rather than a directional certainty toward high exposure.
ESS 2700.d: Students are introduced to the principles and tools of wellness coaching practice. Topics include scope of practice, ethics and values, effective communication, relationship building, and facilitating results to illuminate the discipline of wellness coaching. Research based techniques and best practices for facilitating behavior change are included.

r: Fundamentals of Coaching is an entry-level course built explicitly to satisfy the Colorado High School Activities Association's three-year Letter of Authorization for coaching, covering principles of coaching, creating a healthy and age-appropriate athletic experience, and national sport-coaching standards. The instrumental work task is coaching youth athletes safely, in-person, real-time instruction, physical-development judgment calls, and injury-prevention decisions specific to age and sport. This is a hard, course-specific institutional mandate: the credentialing body requires completion of this coursework to legally coach, independent of whether AI could otherwise perform coaching-knowledge tasks. Verification burden is meaningful because coaching decisions affect youth athlete safety and development. At 24 months, the CHSAA authorization requirement alone keeps instrumental necessity intact regardless of how exposed the underlying content might otherwise be.

By 2031, AI tools may generate generic coaching-principles content or practice-planning templates competently, reflecting the broader pattern of writing- and planning-style tasks scoring high on automation exposure in task-exposure research. But the CHSAA Letter of Authorization requirement is a state athletic-association credentialing mandate tied to this specific course or its equivalent, not merely a knowledge outcome an AI system could replicate, so institutional lock-in continues to cap exposure regardless of content automatability. The course also concerns real-time, in-person coaching of adolescent athletes, an embodied, high-stakes interpersonal activity where verification burden stays meaningfully protective given injury and developmental-safety consequences. Diffusion research indicates institutional credentialing requirements like this tend to change slowly even as underlying capability improves, reinforcing continuity at this horizon.

Looking to 2036, a credentialing body could in principle revise its authorization requirements to accommodate AI-assisted coaching preparation, but there is no current evidence CHSAA or comparable state athletic associations are moving in that direction, and institutional brakes of this kind have historically proven durable even as underlying capability accelerates per METR/Epoch trend data. The embodied, real-time nature of youth-athlete coaching, motivating, correcting technique, and making in-the-moment safety judgments, also remains resistant to substitution regardless of how competent AI becomes at generating coaching-principles content. It would be overconfident to predict this course's elimination given the persistence of its specific institutional mandate; the more defensible expectation is that the certification requirement continues binding this course in place through the horizon, keeping instrumental necessity low-exposure despite rising capability in adjacent informational tasks.
ESS 2720.d: This entry-level class is designed to meet requirements for a three year Letter of Authorization for coaching in the State of Colorado from the Colorado High School Activities Association. This course provides an overview of knowledge and skills in principles of coaching. Students will learn to create a healthy and age appropriate athletic experience along with meeting the national standards for sport coaches based on the most recent National Association of Sport and Physical Education guidelines.

r: This upper-division course covers etiologies, risk factors, and pathophysiology of health conditions, application of the WHO's ICF disability and functioning model, exposure to selected medical tests and diagnostic procedures, and determining when a client needs referral to advanced medical care. The instrumental work task is largely clinical-reasoning and diagnostic-adjacent: interpreting presenting information against pathophysiological knowledge to make a defensible referral judgment, a cognitive task increasingly within reach of medical-domain AI systems per real-deliverable capability research showing top models approaching but still not matching expert performance on real occupational deliverables. However, task-exposure research also finds science- and critical-thinking-heavy work negatively associated with exposure, and referral decisions carry real patient-safety error costs requiring expert verification. These offsetting factors keep near-term instrumental need for this specific course firmly intact.

By 2031, AI clinical-decision-support tools handling pathophysiology-based reasoning and diagnostic-test interpretation are likely to be considerably more capable and more available to exercise-science practitioners, plausibly performing much of the pattern-matching underlying referral decisions competently. This raises real exposure relative to the 24-month horizon. Yet the binding constraint remains verification burden: jagged-frontier research shows that users relying on AI outside a system's true competence become meaningfully less accurate while remaining confident, and misjudging whether a client needs advanced medical care is exactly the kind of high-stakes, non-obvious failure mode that requires a knowledgeable human checking the output. No accreditation or licensure lock-in specifically protects this course, so its rating rises to Medium on rising underlying capability, but the clinical-verification requirement keeps it below High.

At the ten-year horizon, continued progress in medical-domain AI capability, consistent with fast task-time-horizon doubling documented in capability-trend research, makes it plausible that diagnostic-reasoning and pathophysiology-interpretation tasks central to this course become substantially AI-assisted in professional practice, strengthening the case for elevated exposure. This is offered with real hedging, however: science and critical-thinking-intensive work has shown a persistent negative association with automation exposure in task-exposure research, and the referral-judgment core of this course, deciding when a case exceeds an exercise-science practitioner's scope, carries irreducible error costs that argue for continued expert verification regardless of how capable underlying models become. Diffusion of validated clinical-decision tools into this specific practice context will also likely lag raw capability. Medium reflects genuine rising exposure bounded by a durable verification constraint, not a confident forecast of displacement.
ESS 3110.d: Students are introduced to etiologies, risk factors, physiology and pathophysiology of various health conditions. Students learn to use and apply the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) model and, are introduced to selected medical tests, diagnostic procedures. Students also learn how to determine the need for more advanced medical care for individuals with selected health conditions.

r: ESS 3220 teaches students to apply behavioral theories, self-efficacy, stages-of-change, motivational interviewing, to design exercise-adherence interventions, identify client barriers, and sustain motivation for fitness, wellness, and recovery outcomes, mapping to Coaching and Developing Others and Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships. At 24 months, generative tools already draft motivational scripts and adherence plans, and task-exposure research classifies writing- and communication-heavy work as positively associated with exposure. But delivering trust-building, real-time behavior-change conversations with a live client remains an embodied, relational skill that AI does not yet substitute reliably in practice. Diffusion data show only a minority of firms have operationally deployed such tools, so the instrumental need to take this course to perform these tasks competently is only lightly eroded at this horizon. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI coaching apps and chatbots, already emerging in commercial fitness and wellness platforms, are likely to handle more routine adherence coaching, reminder generation, barrier identification via check-in surveys, personalized motivational messaging, pushing realized task automatability from occasional toward common. Productivity research on customer-support-style interactions shows the largest gains accrue to novice practitioners using AI assistance, suggesting entry-level behavior-coaching tasks taught here could increasingly be scaffolded by AI rather than requiring independent mastery. Verification burden stays moderate: erroneous behavior-change advice carries real but not acute stakes, and no licensure or accreditation lock protects the course. The rating rises to Medium as adoption catches up with already-demonstrated capability, though person-to-person motivational rapport with clients facing high barriers likely remains a partially protected niche within the broader curriculum.

Over a ten-year horizon, capability trends, with task-time-horizon doubling roughly every four to seven months, suggest AI systems could plausibly handle most behavioral-theory-application tasks this course teaches: screening client barriers, generating individualized adherence plans, adjusting motivational strategy from progress data, especially as wearable and app-based coaching becomes mainstream. This pushes the base rating to High. This is a genuinely uncertain, long-horizon projection: macro diffusion evidence shows AI adoption spreading unevenly and slowly even where capability exists, and no accreditation or licensure structure protects this course from displacement. The persistent human element is not the behavioral theory itself but the relational trust-building of in-person or synchronous coaching relationships, which may retain some residual instrumental value even as the theoretical content becomes thoroughly AI-deliverable across most settings.
ESS 3220.d: This course is designed for students interested in the sport, fitness, exercise or physical rehabilitation disciplines. In this course, students learn the behavioral aspects of exercise, physical activity, and sport to be more effective in improving fitness, wellness, and recovery outcomes of clients. Students examine behaviors and behavioral theories regarding adherence to exercise, overcoming barriers, and maintaining motivation.

r: ESS 3250 trains students to conduct physical and behavioral screenings, deliver client communication, and design coaching and adherence plans grounded in nutritional and physiological science, mapping to Assisting and Caring for Others and Getting Information via hands-on screening. At 24 months, the physical-screening component, movement assessment and health-history intake requiring hands-on or in-person judgment, keeps embodiment protective, and jagged-frontier research shows AI users perform worse operating outside a model's competence zone, a live risk in individualized physical assessment. Task-exposure research flags writing and communication tasks as more exposed, so plan-writing and follow-up messaging are already assisted by AI, but the course's core hands-on screening and in-person coaching skill is not yet substitutable in any currently deployed practice setting or platform. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI-assisted coaching apps may increasingly automate check-ins, adherence messaging, and even some remote screening triage, but the physical, hands-on screening skills this course emphasizes, postural and movement assessment, in-person client rapport during coaching sessions, remain embodied tasks current and near-term AI cannot substitute directly. Productivity research shows the largest AI-driven gains accrue in text-heavy, lower-skill-entry contexts, describing the administrative side of coaching, documentation, plan drafting, more than the physical-assessment side this course centers. Verification burden stays moderate: poor screening judgments carry real client-safety implications. Because embodiment remains low, screenings and in-person coaching, the dampener holds the rating at Low even as adjacent digital coaching functions become more commonly AI-assisted, reflecting a genuinely uncertain but still-protected middle horizon for this coaching-and-screening curriculum.

At ten years, the balance shifts modestly: capability-trend research on rapidly compounding task-time horizons suggests remote and app-mediated coaching tools may extend into more of the behavioral-planning tasks this course covers, even as hands-on physical screening remains comparatively resistant. Diffusion data indicate real-world adoption lags capability significantly, so any such shift would likely be partial and uneven across fitness and rehabilitation settings. No licensure or accreditation lock protects this course specifically, so the analysis rests on the durability of embodiment as a protective factor. Given persistent uncertainty about how much physical screening and in-person coaching work migrates to app-mediated or wearable-driven models over a decade, this rating is offered with real hedging: Medium reflects the base capability trajectory while embodiment still tempers full displacement.
ESS 3250.d: In this course, students apply health coaching concepts for practitioners specifically working in the fitness, exercise, and physical rehabilitation related fields. Students survey nutritional and physiological sciences, behavioral and physical screenings, client communication, motivation, planning and adherence strategies, which provides them with a background in fitness and exercise coaching.

r: ESS 3300 teaches qualitative analysis of joint motion, musculoskeletal mechanics, and application of physics principles to human movement, explicitly framed toward teaching effectiveness in physical education, athletic training, and exercise science, mapping to Analyzing Data and Training and Teaching Others but grounded in hands-on movement observation. Task-exposure research finds science- and critical-thinking-heavy skills negatively associated with AI exposure, fitting this course's applied-mechanics content. Movement analysis in practice requires observing a live body performing an activity and diagnosing joint-level mechanics in real time, an embodied task where jagged-frontier findings show AI users markedly less accurate outside a model's competence zone. With BIO 2310 as prerequisite and the course itself feeding subsequent applied coursework in exercise science, foundational scaffolding further protects it at this horizon. Rating Low.

At five years, video-based motion-capture and computer-vision tools may assist qualitative movement analysis in research or clinical settings, but the course's instructional purpose, training students to personally observe, diagnose, and teach joint mechanics to future physical education, athletic training, and exercise-science practitioners, still depends on embodied clinical judgment that AI augmentation does not yet replace at the point of skill acquisition. No licensure-specific mandate protects the course, but its role as prerequisite substrate, required after BIO 2310 and feeding exercise physiology and biomechanics coursework, caps any rise at Medium regardless of capability growth, per the foundational-scaffolding constraint. Given continued low embodiment and low verification tolerance for movement diagnosis, the rating remains Low, though AI-assisted motion-analysis tools in adjacent professional practice are an emerging trend worth watching.

Ten years out, capability trajectories, rapid task-time-horizon doubling, could plausibly bring markerless motion-capture and AI movement-diagnosis tools into mainstream athletic-training and physical-education practice, meaningfully raising realized task automatability for movement assessment generally.
